findings.title: Brand Name Typo Returns Zero Results — No Correction
findings.impact_stat: 12% of all searches contain typos (Baymard Institute search UX research)
findings.actual_behavior: ZERO results. No correction prompt. No recovery. Screenshot: 236KB for 'handbags' vs 227KB for this query — sparse page confirmed.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia's typo-tolerant indexing automatically corrects 1-2 character transpositions including micheal→michael. No configuration required for standard typos; brand-specific variants handled via Synonym Rules.
findings.expected_behavior: Typo-corrected results for 'michael kors bag' with 'Did you mean' prompt
findings.prospect_description: The brand's own most common misspelling — 'micheal' (i/e transposition of 'michael') — returns a dead end. Every shopper who types the brand's own name in this common variant loses the ability to browse, find, or purchase.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: +150% sales contribution from search; -88% search bounce rate

findings.title: Brand Monogram 'MK' Returns Zero Results
findings.actual_behavior: ZERO results (DOM confirmed). 192KB file size vs 244KB for full 'Michael Kors Collection' query — near-empty page confirmed.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia Synonym Rules with one-way mapping: MK → Michael Kors. This is a 5-minute configuration that permanently solves the brand monogram discovery gap.
findings.expected_behavior: Full Michael Kors monogram collection — wallets, bag charms, keyrings, MK-branded accessories
findings.prospect_description: The MK monogram is printed on every Michael Kors product. It is the brand's most visible symbol. Shoppers typing 'MK bag,' 'MK tote,' or 'MK wallet' — highest-intent, brand-loyal customers — receive nothing.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: Conversion rate doubled for search users; 80% mobile traffic handled

findings.title: Gifting Intent Query Returns Zero Results
findings.actual_behavior: ZERO results (DOM confirmed). No NLP parsing of gifting intent, recipient, or price constraint.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia NeuralSearch parses: intent=gift, recipient=her, price_constraint=<$300, and returns gift-appropriate accessories filtered by price. No custom rules required — NeuralSearch understands natural language intent natively.
findings.expected_behavior: Curated accessories under $300 for gifting occasions — handbags, jewelry, accessories filtered by price and occasion
findings.prospect_description: The most common luxury gifting query pattern — used throughout holiday, Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, and anniversary shopping seasons — returns nothing. SFCC treats this as a literal keyword match. No product is named 'gift for her under 300.'
findings.algolia_case_study_result: +37% conversion rate improvement after deploying Algolia

findings.title: Multi-Attribute NLP Query Returns Zero Results
findings.actual_behavior: ZERO results (DOM confirmed). 122KB page — confirmed near-empty. SFCC cannot parse 3 simultaneous attributes from natural language.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia NeuralSearch decomposes multi-attribute queries into structured filters: color=black AND material=leather AND category=handbags. Automatic — no custom rules required.
findings.expected_behavior: Black leather handbags filtered by color + material + use-case simultaneously
findings.prospect_description: The shopper knows exactly what they want. SFCC literal match cannot parse multi-attribute intent. This is the highest-intent, highest-conversion shopper archetype — and they hit a wall.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: +1.47% site conversion rate (A/B test); +2% lift in conversions

findings.title: No Federated Search — Content Pages Invisible
findings.actual_behavior: Hardcoded URL redirect to returns/exchange page — not federated search. Content pages are not indexed in the search engine. Products shown instead of policy content.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia Federated Search indexes multiple data sources — products, content pages, help articles, store locator — and surfaces them in a single unified SAYT and results interface with labeled sections.
findings.expected_behavior: Returns/exchange policy content page surfaced alongside or instead of products
findings.prospect_description: Customer service queries typed into search return products instead of content. For a luxury brand where post-purchase experience drives retention, this creates friction at the moment shoppers most need help.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: Personalized stylist experience; capabilities 'way beyond what they thought was possible'

findings.title: Text-Only SAYT — No Product Images or Rich Content
findings.actual_behavior: Text suggestions only. 2 category links. No product images. doyoumean class present but 0 children — no typo correction in SAYT either. Shopping Muse not activated during search (visible:false).
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia InstantSearch with federated SAYT — product thumbnails, category shortcuts, editorial content, and help links in a single brand-styled dropdown with sub-60ms response.
findings.expected_behavior: Rich SAYT with product thumbnails, category chips, trending searches, editorial content in single dropdown
findings.prospect_description: On a luxury brand, the SAYT dropdown is the first visual interaction with search. Text-only suggestions lose the brand aesthetic advantage at the moment shoppers are most engaged — about to commit to a query.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: Algolia luxury search infrastructure across global luxury conglomerate brands

findings.title: Zero Search Personalization — Shopping Muse Inactive During Search
findings.impact_stat: 0% of luxury ecommerce sites offer personalization vs 41% of apparel sites broadly (Baymard Institute luxury research estimate)
findings.actual_behavior: Identical results for all shoppers. Shopping Muse DOM present (dy-muse-suggestions-wrapper) but visible:false during regular search. No behavioral signals in search result ranking.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia AI Personalization re-ranks search results based on each shopper's behavioral signals. Works alongside Dynamic Yield — Algolia handles search ranking personalization, DY handles chat and downstream recommendations.
findings.expected_behavior: Personalized result ranking based on browse/purchase history — handbag results prioritized after browsing handbags category
findings.prospect_description: Zero personalization in the search layer. Every shopper sees identical results regardless of their browse history, purchase history, or price affinity. Shopping Muse personalizes only the chat layer — the search bar has no AI.

findings.title: Merchandising Consistency Gap — Search vs Category Browse
findings.actual_behavior: Search 'handbags' (236KB) vs /handbags category URL (90KB) — 2.6x content size difference. Divergent product volumes or rendering between the two entry paths.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia's unified Rules Engine applies the same merchandising logic to both search and browse — one configuration, consistent experience across all entry points.
findings.expected_behavior: Same products, same ordering, consistent merchandising between search results and category browse
findings.prospect_description: SFCC search and category browse use separate rules engines. Merchandisers must manage two separate configurations for the same products — doubling operational overhead and creating inconsistent shopper experiences depending on how they arrive at a category.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: +210% increase in search usage after deploying Algolia

findings.title: Sparse PDP Recommendations — Limited Cross-Sell
findings.impact_stat: Average Algolia customer sees a 15% increase in AOV (Algolia fashion industry page)
findings.actual_behavior: Recommendations present (DOM confirmed) but sparse — 91KB PDP page vs Costco 400KB+. No evidence of advanced FBT or ML-powered cross-sell carousel.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia Recommend with Frequently Bought Together and Related Products models — trained on historical purchase and browse data to surface highest-conversion cross-sell items.
findings.expected_behavior: ML-powered Frequently Bought Together, related styles, cross-sell accessories carousel on PDP
findings.prospect_description: For a luxury accessories brand where cross-sell (bag + wallet + keyring + sunglasses) is core to basket size, weak PDP recommendations directly limit AOV per transaction. Shoppers who would purchase complementary items are not being shown them.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: +2% lift in conversions using Algolia Recommend + Search + DRR

findings.title: Search Analytics Disconnected from Adobe Analytics
findings.actual_behavior: Some analytics labels present (bestseller/trending/popular in DOM) but likely manually merchandised. Adobe Analytics is the analytics platform and is entirely separate from search — not feeding ranking or SAYT.
findings.algolia_solution: Algolia Search Analytics and Query Suggestions create an automated feedback loop: what shoppers search → what they click → what gets promoted in SAYT and results. No manual curation required for trending signals.
findings.expected_behavior: Real-time CTR-weighted trending, search analytics feeding result ranking and SAYT suggestions automatically
findings.prospect_description: John Idol has stated significant investment in data analytics capabilities. That investment and the search engine are siloed systems — shopper behavior data in Adobe Analytics does not flow into search result ranking or SAYT suggestions.
findings.algolia_case_study_result: +210% increase in search usage (engagement compound from analytics-driven relevance)

# Loom Video Script — Michael Kors Search Audit

**Format:** 2-minute max (120 seconds)
**Word count target:** 200-280 words
**Presenter:** [AE Name], Algolia

---

## HOOK (0–10 seconds)

"I spent 30 minutes on michaelkors.com and found four things that should not be happening on a brand with three consecutive quarters of traffic recovery."

---

## DEMO (10–90 seconds)

**[Show screenshot: screenshots/09b-intent-mk-abbreviation.png]**

"This is what I see when I type 'MK' into the search bar on michaelkors.com. MK — the brand's own monogram, printed on every handbag, wallet, and keyring you sell. Zero results. No products. No correction. Just empty."

*[Transition: move to next screenshot]*

"That's not a fluke. Here's what happens with the most common luxury gifting query."

**[Show screenshot: screenshots/13-nlp-gift-for-her.png]**

"'Gift for her under 300' — the phrase that drives 15 to 25 percent of luxury accessories purchases during every major shopping season. Zero results. SFCC processes this as a literal keyword match. No product is named 'gift for her under 300,' so the search engine returns nothing."

*[Transition: move to next screenshot]*

"One more."

**[Show screenshot: screenshots/05-typo-micheal-kors-bag.png]**

"'Micheal kors bag' — the most common misspelling of the brand name, the i-e transposition. Zero results. No 'did you mean.' The brand's own name, misspelled the way most people misspell it, hits a dead end."

*[Transition: back to presenter]*

"Three gaps. There are four total. On $566M in digital revenue with a 15% search engagement rate, fixing these gaps is worth $21 million a year on a conservative model using industry benchmarks."

strategic_angles.hook: No direct competitor has deployed AI search. Michael Kors can own the discovery experience in accessible luxury before Coach, Kate Spade, or Tory Burch act.
strategic_angles.label: Greenfield First-Mover in Accessible Luxury
strategic_angles.algolia_proof: 75% of top fashion brands use Algolia — the category is standardizing. First-mover in accessible luxury is still available.
strategic_angles.discovery_question: Are you aware that none of your direct competitors have deployed a dedicated AI search platform yet? What does first-mover mean to Michael Kors in digital discovery?
strategic_angles.objection: We're an accessible-luxury brand built on curated JetSet storytelling and editorial merchandising — our customers browse the narrative, they don't search like a mass-market retailer. A heavy AI-search investment doesn't fit how luxury discovery actually works for us.
strategic_angles.objection_counter: TAG Heuer — a luxury accessories brand with the same handbag / watch / jewelry positioning as Michael Kors — doubled its conversion rate for search users after deploying Algolia (algolia.com/customers/tag-heuer). Luxury shoppers who do reach for the search bar are the most intent-rich, highest-converting segment; storytelling and search are not either/or. And because no direct competitor (Coach, Kate Spade, Tory Burch) has deployed a dedicated AI-search platform yet, the first-mover position in accessible luxury is still open — for now.

strategic_angles.hook: Corey Moran (Google, AI background) starts April 6. New CMOs audit the tech stack in the first 90 days. Get Algolia on the roadmap before the audit — not after.

pain_points: New CMO will find 4 CRITICAL zero-result patterns

strategic_angles.algolia_proof: Algolia SFCC connector deploys in weeks. By the time the new CMO conducts a formal stack audit, Algolia can be live and showing results.
strategic_angles.discovery_question: What does your current search experience story look like for Corey Moran's first week? Would it be better to have a fix in progress or a problem to explain?
strategic_angles.objection: A new CMO landing April 6 won't sign off on a net-new search vendor in her first quarter — new leadership does listening tours and freezes discretionary spend before committing capital, especially mid-turnaround. Capri is already directing roughly $300–350M into Michael Kors store renovations and a footwear repositioning; net-new martech is not where that capital is going.
strategic_angles.objection_counter: Corey Moran comes from Google with an AI-driven personalization background, so she recognizes search as a revenue lever on day one rather than a line item to defer. The ask isn't a capital project competing with store renovations: the Algolia SFCC connector deploys in weeks, making search a fast, self-funding conversion win she can put on the board inside her first 90 days — a fix in progress rather than a 1.9/10 search score she has to explain.

strategic_angles.hook: Three sequential quarters of traffic improvement (John Idol, Q3 FY2026). Traffic is recovering. If that traffic lands on a search engine where 'MK' returns zero results, recovery stalls at the conversion funnel.
strategic_angles.label: Brand Recovery — Traffic Improvement Needs Search Conversion
pain_points: Brand's own monogram unrecognized by search
strategic_angles.algolia_proof: Conservative scenario: $21.37M/year in recoverable revenue. The $4B revenue target requires every digital conversion lever to work. Search is the highest-leverage tool and it's never been built.
strategic_angles.discovery_question: You have three quarters of traffic improvement — are you seeing search conversion improve in parallel, or is it lagging?
strategic_angles.objection: Our biggest issue isn't search. On the record, John Idol has said 'our biggest issue inside the company actually is not the accessories, it's our footwear' — we're focused on product repositioning, pricing, and store renovations, and that's where the turnaround gets won. Site search isn't the priority.
strategic_angles.objection_counter: Product and search aren't competing priorities — the footwear repositioning and three straight quarters of traffic improvement only convert if the site turns that recovered traffic into sales, and today the search bar returns zero results for the brand's own 'MK' monogram. Idol's stated goal — 'We are confident in our ability to grow Michael Kors to $4 billion in revenue' — requires every conversion lever to work; the ~$21M conservative recoverable-revenue estimate is upside that sits alongside, not inside, the store capex budget.

strategic_angles.hook: John Idol: 'We spent a lot of time and money on data analytics.' But Adobe Analytics and search are siloed systems. The analytics investment cannot deliver its stated purpose — deeper personal connections — through a keyword-match search engine.
strategic_angles.label: Analytics Investment Needs a Search Layer to Deliver ROI
pain_points: No real-time signal loop from search behavior
Trending suggestions likely static, not analytics-driven
strategic_angles.algolia_proof: Algolia Search Analytics creates the feedback loop: shopper behavior → real-time ranking signals → smarter suggestions. The analytics investment finally connects to the conversion layer.
strategic_angles.discovery_question: What percentage of your search behavior data from Adobe Analytics flows back into your search ranking or trending suggestions today?
strategic_angles.objection: We've already spent heavily on data analytics and Adobe — adding another platform risks creating a new silo and more integration overhead, not less. We'd rather get more out of the Adobe stack we already own than bolt on a separate search vendor.
strategic_angles.objection_counter: Idol himself framed the gap: 'we spent a lot of time and money and have the resources around our data analytics to really give us the tools to be able to engage with new and existing consumers.' But analytics can only act on behavior it can see, and a keyword-match search engine emits no structured search-intent signal to feed back. Algolia is the layer that turns search behavior into the real-time ranking signal Adobe can then act on — it makes the existing analytics investment finally reach the conversion moment, rather than duplicating it.

recommended_first_play.detail: Pivotree built and hosts the michaelkors.com Oracle/SFCC headless stack and has a named relationship with Ann Marie Ippoliti (VP Ecommerce). This is the highest-probability, fastest path to a qualified first meeting — faster than cold outreach.
recommended_first_play.headline: Warm intro via Pivotree SI
